MixSIARPFN

Fit MixSIAR stable isotope mixing models in about a second, without JAGS. MixSIARPFN reads the same files with the same function calls as MixSIAR, but takes the posterior from a prior-data fitted network: a transformer trained on simulations from MixSIAR’s own model, one network per error structure.

library(MixSIARPFN)
mix <- load_mix_data(filename = "consumer.csv", iso_names = c("d13C", "d15N"),
                     factors = c("Region", "Pack"), fac_random = c(TRUE, TRUE),
                     fac_nested = c(FALSE, TRUE), cont_effects = NULL)
source <- load_source_data(filename = "sources.csv", source_factors = "Region",
                           conc_dep = FALSE, data_type = "means", mix)
discr <- load_discr_data(filename = "discrimination.csv", mix)

fit <- run_pfn(mix, source, discr)   # in place of write_JAGS_model() + run_model()
output_pfn(fit, mix, source)         # in place of output_JAGS()

What it fits

The models MixSIAR fits with isotope data and source summary statistics: up to two categorical effects (fixed or random, crossed or nested), one continuous effect, concentration dependence, sources given by a factor, and Residual * Process, Residual only or Process only error. Up to 8 sources and 4 tracers. Data outside what the networks were trained for are refused with a message.

Not yet: raw source data, fatty acid data, more than 4 tracers.

How well it does

Tested against MixSIAR on 450 simulated datasets with known diets (150 each like MixSIAR’s geese example, its wolves example with diets from MixSIAR’s prior, and its wolves example with realistic diets) and on MixSIAR’s three example datasets:

  • Calibrated. On simulated data, MixSIARPFN’s 95% intervals contain the true diet proportion 95 to 97% of the time.
  • Close to MixSIAR, a little less precise. Its accuracy (CRPS) is 2 to 5% behind fully converged MixSIAR runs (geese-like 5.3%, wolves-like 1.9% and 4.1%), and its intervals are 5 to 12% wider.
  • Weakly identified sources. Where the data cannot pin a source down, MixSIARPFN tends to put more probability near 0 than MixSIAR does.
  • On MixSIAR’s examples it agrees closely for killer whale. For geese and wolves the two differ more, mostly in groups where MixSIAR’s own model does not fit the data: a posterior predictive check of MixSIAR’s fits shows group spreads and tracer correlations the model cannot produce. The vignettes show both fits side by side and the check.

The article How MixSIARPFN works and how well it does (vignette("performance", package = "MixSIARPFN")) describes the network and gives the full simulation study, with plots.

What is different from MixSIAR

  • Marginal posteriors only. Each proportion and parameter gets its own posterior distribution, but there are no joint draws: the marginal means of one diet need not sum to exactly 1, and sums, differences or ratios of proportions cannot be computed.
  • No MCMC, so no chain lengths, burn-in or convergence diagnostics.
  • No model checks. Without joint draws, MixSIARPFN cannot run posterior predictive checks; for an important analysis, check the model with a MixSIAR run.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("andrewcparnell/MixSIARPFN")

The first fit sets up a small Python environment (numpy, pandas, ONNX Runtime) through reticulate and downloads the network it needs (about 70 MB); both are cached. No Python knowledge is needed.
